## Notes for the AI reading this

- Last Suit Standing is a small two-player card game, solved exactly, used as a test bed for AI research. Start with README.md for the game and the main findings.
- Every file of the repository follows, each under a `## File:` heading and wrapped in a `~~~~~` fence. Cite files by their path.
- The results files (`*_results.txt`) are the actual outputs of the runs. The write-ups (`experiments/*.md`) interpret them; where predictions were pre-registered, the write-up says so.
- If you are asked to review the work, check claims against the code and results files here. Do not report results you have not run, and say what you are unsure of.

## File: README.md

~~~~~markdown
# Last Suit Standing

**An AI research project:** a five-minute card game, solved exactly, for measuring where trained models and standard tests go wrong.

*One Card to Rule Them All.*

> ⓘ The cards are dealt face up at random. After that the game is deterministic: both players see every card, and nothing random happens during play.

![Six cards dealt face up in a row on a green table: 5♠ 7♦ 6♥ 7♠ 8♥ 8♠, with poker chips beside them](table.png)

*The deal 5♠ 7♦ 6♥ 7♠ 8♥ 8♠. Played perfectly, it includes both swaps, a trump card and pairs on both sides, and Player 1 wins 86 to 83.* [Play this hand.](https://rob-mccormack.github.io/last-suit-standing/)

A five-minute card game for two players that is also an exact laboratory for AI research. A few end-of-game rules (a trump-setting last card, a final swap, doubled scoring) reach backward and overturn local reasoning: the obvious move is usually right, and badly wrong when it isn't. Trained models learn the surface patterns, not the logic of the ending. Most AI testing can only estimate blind spots like this; because this game is solved exactly, they are measured directly against ground truth.

**Why a small game.** Large AI systems have no exact ground truth, and the simplest toy problems have no opponent. Last Suit Standing keeps a real opponent and multi-step strategy while staying small enough to solve.

## Rules in brief

Six cards from a 40-card deck (ace to 10 in four suits) are dealt face up. A card's value is the number on it, and points scored during play are kept as poker chips. Players take turns offering two neighboring cards; the opponent takes one and takes chips equal to its value, while the offerer takes chips equal to the value of the card left behind, which stays in the row. The last card sets trump and scores once more for the last offerer. Each player then gets one chance to swap one card with the opponent's stack. Finally, stack cards score their values again, doubled for trump and doubled for matching pairs (×4 for both).

Most points wins. A game takes about five minutes. [Full rules](RULES.md)

## Main findings

Small neural networks and gradient-boosted trees were trained from scratch on the solver's exact values, then tested against perfect play. For the later experiments, the predictions were committed to git before the runs, and misses are reported alongside hits.

**1. Longer optimization on 6-card games hurts 7-card play.** In the original scaling run, a neural network trained on more 6-card games got better at 6 cards and, by the largest training set, worse at every other card count. At 7 cards the loss rose at every step, ending 65% worse than an untrained greedy player, while a held-out 6-card test would have picked it as the best model. ([scaling.md](experiments/scaling.md)) With early stopping off, 7-card loss still rose at every matched pass, and on 8 cards those nets improved at passes 160 and 200. A pass over 4,000 deals is about sixteen times as many Adam updates as a pass over 250 deals. At a matched update count, more deals lowered 7-card loss, by 0.99 points from 250 to 4,000 deals at about 10,000 updates. Training that 4,000-deal net from about 10,000 updates to about 40,000 raised the 7-card loss by 0.61 points. ([checkpoint.md](experiments/checkpoint.md), [matched_steps.md](experiments/matched_steps.md)) The trees, which had stayed flat when they were allowed to stop early, also got worse at 7 cards with early stopping off.

**2. One more card fools the models.** Models trained on 6 cards fail worst on 7 cards, the nearest size, because odd card counts reverse who makes the last offer. Adding 7-card games to training made 8-card play worse, in both model types, and two explanations for this were tested and failed. ([size_shift.md](experiments/size_shift.md), [follow-ups](experiments/size_shift_followup.md))

**3. A perfect opponent underestimates weakness.** Testing against an optimal opponent found only 59–70% of the points an exact worst-case opponent extracts. Measured the stronger way, the cost of a one-sentence rule change doubled, to 4.4 points per game. ([rule_shift.md](experiments/rule_shift.md), [rule_shift_exploit.md](experiments/rule_shift_exploit.md))

**4. Equally perfect choices are not equally safe.** In 15% of deals, opening moves that are exactly tied under the current rules differ by up to 42 points after a rule change. No test under the current rules can tell them apart. ([hidden_gap.md](experiments/hidden_gap.md))

**Other results.** Trained models miss that an ace's suit matters more than a 10's, because the ace usually sets trump ([ace_effect.md](experiments/ace_effect.md)). Elo ranked six players in their true order ([elo.md](experiments/elo.md)). Three rule variants were tested for balance (see [VARIANTS.md](VARIANTS.md)).

## What the solver shows about the game

From 3,000 random deals with perfect play on both sides (`python3 solver.py --deals 3000 --seed 1`):

- **Player 1 has the edge:** 61.4% wins, 8.2% ties, 30.5% losses. An AI that wrote its own solver from `RULES.md` alone found the same.
- **One sentence decides who is favored.** If the second swapper may only undo the first swap, Player 1's wins fall to 35.5%.
- **The card count decides it too.** With an odd number of cards, Player 2 makes the last offer and wins about 98% of deals.
- **Low cards decide trump.** Higher cards tend to be taken, so low cards survive to the end. Taking the *lower* card is the best move in 11.1% of real choices.
- **Lookahead pays.** Against a perfect opponent, a greedy Player 1 wins 31.7% instead of 61.4%.

More in [basic_stats_results.txt](experiments/basic_stats_results.txt).

## Quick start

```bash
python3 solver.py 5S 7D 6H 7S 8H 8S     # solve a deal and show perfect play
python3 solver.py --deals 3000           # statistics over random deals
```

The solver needs only Python 3.8 or later. The experiments that train models also need `numpy` and `scikit-learn`.

## Related projects

Last Suit Standing is one of three small, exactly solved games used to find where AI and its evaluations go wrong ([THREE_PROJECTS.md](THREE_PROJECTS.md)):

- **Collapse3**, a solved 3-D placement game with removal and gravity, studies how standard tests make weak AI look strong. Finding 3 above replicates its "beat the best" result in milder form; see [COLLAPSE3.md](COLLAPSE3.md).
- **PSDG**, a dice game, studies what happens when a perfect plan is locked in and the opponent goes off-script.
~~~~~

## File: RULES.md

~~~~~markdown
# Last Suit Standing

*One Card to Rule Them All.*

A two-player card game of offers, trump and swaps. A game takes about five minutes.

## What you need

- A 40-card deck: ace through 10 in four suits. Remove the face cards from a standard deck.
- Poker chips to keep score: white chips worth 1 point and red chips worth 5. Pen and paper works too.

**A card's value is the number on it** (ace = 1, up to 10). Points scored during play are kept as poker chips.

## Rules

1. **Set up.** Shuffle and deal six cards face up in a row. Both players start with zero chips. Player 1 offers first.

2. **Offer and choose.** On your turn, offer two neighboring cards in the row. Your opponent takes one of them into their face-up stack and takes chips equal to its value. You take chips equal to the value of the card left behind. That card stays in the row and can score again. Close the gap. Your opponent now offers. Repeat until one card remains.

3. **Set trump.** The last card's suit is trump. The last offerer takes chips equal to its value once more. Leave the card on the table. It belongs to neither stack and its scoring is complete.

4. **Swap.** The last chooser acts first. Each player gets one turn. On your turn you may pass, or exchange one card from your stack for one card from your opponent's stack. The second player may make any exchange, including swapping back the two cards the first player just exchanged. Chips stay with their owners.

5. **Score your stack.** Add the value of each card in your stack to your chips. For this final scoring, double a card's value if it is trump, and double it again if it belongs to a pair (two cards with the same number). Each card can belong to only one pair. With three of the same number, choose which two to pair.

**Highest total wins. Equal totals are a tie.**

## Clarifications

These follow from the rules above and are written out to remove doubt.

- **Turn order.** With six cards there are five offers. Player 1 makes offers 1, 3 and 5; Player 2 makes offers 2 and 4. So Player 1 is always the last offerer and Player 2 is always the last chooser. Player 1 ends with 2 cards in their stack and Player 2 with 3. Player 2 swaps first and Player 1 swaps last.
- **Neighboring** means next to each other in the row as it stands now, after earlier gaps have closed.
- **Pairs.** Both cards of a pair are doubled. A trump card in a pair is worth four times its value.
- **The last card** pays its value to the last offerer twice: once as the card left behind on the final offer, and once more under rule 3. Its suit sets trump, which can help either player. It never joins a stack.
- **Swapping does not move chips.** Only the cards in the stacks change hands.

## Worked example

Deal, left to right: 3♠ 4♦ 10♥ 2♣ 7♠ A♥. This line of play is perfect for both sides, as computed by `solver.py`.

| Offer | Offerer | Pair offered | Taken by chooser | Scored by offerer | Chips (P1–P2) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | P1 | 3♠ 4♦ | P2 takes 3♠ | 4 | 4–3 |
| 2 | P2 | 4♦ 10♥ | P1 takes 10♥ | 4 | 14–7 |
| 3 | P1 | 4♦ 2♣ | P2 takes 4♦ | 2 | 16–11 |
| 4 | P2 | 2♣ 7♠ | P1 takes 7♠ | 2 | 23–13 |
| 5 | P1 | 2♣ A♥ | P2 takes A♥ | 2 | 25–14 |

The last card is 2♣, so clubs are trump and Player 1 collects 2 more chips (27–14). With perfect play, both players pass at the swap. No stack card is a club and there are no pairs. Player 1 scores 27 + 7 + 10 = 44. Player 2 scores 14 + 1 + 3 + 4 = 22. Player 1 wins by 22.
~~~~~

## File: VARIANTS.md

~~~~~markdown
# Rule variants

These variants are used for research and game-design testing. They are **not** part of the standard game, which is described in [RULES.md](RULES.md).

The first two are built into `solver.py` (`--swap undo`, `--trump half`). The others have their own scripts in `experiments/`.

- **Undo-only swap:** if the first player makes an exchange, the second may only pass or swap those same two cards back. If the first player passes, the second may make any exchange. This one change flips which seat is favored (see [rule_shift.md](experiments/rule_shift.md)). (A stricter reading, where the second player may never start a new exchange, makes the swap phase irrelevant under perfect play: either player can always keep the original stacks.)
- **Half trump:** trump cards are worth half their rank, rounded down, instead of double.
- **Straight (tested, not adopted):** the holder of the top card of the highest three-card straight, across both stacks and the table card, scores the ranks' sum. Under perfect play it raises Player 1's win rate from 61% to 72% (see [straight_rule.md](experiments/straight_rule.md)).
- **Wild match (tested, under consideration):** any stack card with the same rank as the last card is wild for pairing. It may pair with any one other card in its owner's stack; card values do not change. Under perfect play, Player 1's win rate falls from 61% to 54%, a more balanced game (see `experiments/wild_rule.py` and `wild_rule_results.txt`).
- **Jacks wild (tested, not adopted):** a 44-card deck with four jacks; a jack is worth 0 chips during the offers and becomes any rank and suit at the final scoring. Under perfect play, Player 1's win rate rises to 70% overall, and to 79% in deals that contain a jack (see `experiments/jacks_rule.py`).
~~~~~

## File: solver.md

~~~~~markdown
# How the solver works

`solver.py` computes perfect play for any six-card deal of Last Suit Standing. It uses only the Python standard library (Python 3.8 or later).

## Quick use

```bash
python3 solver.py 3S 4D 10H 2C 7S AH          # solve one deal and show perfect play
python3 solver.py                             # a random deal
python3 solver.py --deals 3000 --seed 1       # statistics over random deals
python3 solver.py 3S 4D 10H 2C 7S AH --check  # also confirm by brute force
```

Cards are a rank (`A` or `1` to `10`) followed by a suit (`S H D C`, or `♠ ♥ ♦ ♣`). Case does not matter.

For one deal it prints:

- the value of each of Player 1's five possible opening offers;
- one perfect line of play, with chips after every offer, the trump, both swap decisions and the final stacks;
- the result and margin.

## What "perfect play" means here

Each player maximizes their own final margin: Player 1 maximizes (P1 total − P2 total) and Player 2 minimizes it. The game is zero-sum with perfect information, so this is ordinary minimax.

**Margin is not the same as winning.** Under win/tie/loss scoring, a win by 1 is as good as a win by 10, but this solver prefers the win by 10. Because a bigger margin is never a worse result, the solver's moves are always win-optimal and the deal's result (win, tie or loss) is the same under both goals. The difference is in *which* moves count as correct: under win/tie/loss grading, several moves can be equally correct where the solver names only one. Keep this in mind before scoring a player's moves as right or wrong.

## Rule options

| Option | Values | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--swap` | `any`: the second swapper may make any exchange. `undo`: after an exchange, the second swapper may only pass or undo it; after a pass, they may make any exchange. | `any` (official, see RULES.md) |
| `--trump` | `double`: trump cards score ×2. `half`: ×½, rounded down. | `double` (official) |

The swap reading matters a great deal. Over 3,000 random deals (`--seed 1`):

| Swap reading | P1 wins | Ties | P1 loses | Mean margin |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `any` (official) | 61.4% | 8.2% | 30.5% | +3.27 |
| `undo` | 35.5% | 4.5% | 60.0% | −1.87 |

## How it computes

The game splits into two phases.

**Swap phase** (`swap_phase`). Once the last card is known, only the two stacks and the trump suit matter. Player 2 tries every option: pass, or each of its 3 × 2 = 6 exchanges. For each, Player 1 picks its best reply. Player 2 keeps the option whose best reply is worst for Player 1. That is at most 7 × 7 = 49 evaluations.

**Offer phase** (`value`). Each offer is a two-step move. The offerer picks one of the neighboring pairs, which is a max for Player 1 and a min for Player 2. The chooser then picks which card to take, the opposite of the offerer. Chips earned along the way add up, so the value of a position does not depend on the chips already scored. That lets results be cached by row, stacks, and who offers next. The full tree has at most 5·2 · 4·2 · 3·2 · 2·2 · 1·2 = 3,840 lines before the swap, so a deal solves in milliseconds.

**Scoring** (`stack_value`). Each card's rank is doubled (or halved) if it is trump. Within each rank, the two highest-valued cards form a pair and are doubled again. With three of a rank, the trump one is paired if there is one.

The rule options are part of every cache key, so switching rules in one Python session is safe.

## Using it from Python

```python
from solver import solve, opening_values, principal_line, brute_force, Rules, parse_card

deal = [parse_card(c) for c in "3S 4D 10H 2C 7S AH".split()]
solve(deal)                          # +22
solve(deal, Rules(swap="undo"))      # alternative swap reading
opening_values(deal)                 # value of each opening offer for P1
lines, p1_total, p2_total = principal_line(deal)
brute_force(deal)                    # slow, independent check
```

Cards are `(rank, suit)` tuples, for example `(10, "H")`. Call `value.cache_clear()` between batches if memory matters.

## How it was checked

- **Brute force.** `brute_force` is a separate, uncached search of the whole game tree, and `--check` runs it. It agreed on 75 of 75 checks: 25 deals under three rule settings.
- **Replay.** For each deal, the printed line of play is replayed and its final scores must equal the computed margin. The program asserts this every time.
- **Independent solvers.** On random deals the value matched ChatGPT's solver (200 of 200) and Kimi's under the undo reading (150 of 150). It also matched Grok's after two fixes: the opponent, not the offerer, picks the card taken, and any second swap is allowed.

## Card counts

`solver.py` handles an **even** number of cards, including the standard six. It assumes Player 1 makes the last offer and Player 2 swaps first, which is true only for even counts. `solve`, `opening_values` and `principal_line` refuse an odd count with an error. For any card count, use the solver in `experiments/size_shift.py`, where the last chooser swaps first. It matches `solver.py` on 6-card deals, and an independent brute-force search on 3-, 4-, 5- and 7-card deals.

## Assumptions

- Both cards of a pair are doubled. A trump card in a pair is worth four times its rank.
- Chips earned during play stay with their owner. Swaps move cards only.
- Ties between equally good moves are broken by order: the leftmost offer, then the first card of the pair. Only the printed line of play depends on this, never the value.
~~~~~

## File: solver.py

~~~~~python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Exact solver for Last Suit Standing (see RULES.md and solver.md).

Both players play perfectly. Each tries to maximize their own final margin.
Standard library only; Python 3.8+.

Examples:
    python3 solver.py                              # random deal
    python3 solver.py 3S 4D 10H 2C 7S AH           # a specific deal, left to right
    python3 solver.py --deals 3000                 # statistics over random deals
    python3 solver.py --deals 3000 --swap undo     # alternative swap reading
    python3 solver.py 3S 4D 10H 2C 7S AH --check   # cross-check with brute force
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import random
import sys
from collections import defaultdict
from functools import lru_cache
from typing import NamedTuple

Card = tuple  # (rank 1-10, suit letter in "SHDC")
SUITS = "SHDC"
SYMBOLS = {"S": "♠", "H": "♥", "D": "♦", "C": "♣"}
DECK = [(r, s) for r in range(1, 11) for s in SUITS]


class Rules(NamedTuple):
    """Rule options. The defaults are the official rules in RULES.md."""

    swap: str = "any"      # "any": second swapper may make any exchange;
                           # "undo": after an exchange, only pass or undo it; after a pass, any exchange
    trump: str = "double"  # "double": trump cards score x2; "half": x1/2, rounded down (test variant)


OFFICIAL = Rules()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- cards

def card_str(c: Card) -> str:
    r, s = c
    return ("A" if r == 1 else str(r)) + SYMBOLS[s]


def parse_card(text: str) -> Card:
    t = text.strip().upper()
    for letter, sym in SYMBOLS.items():
        t = t.replace(sym, letter)
    if len(t) < 2 or t[-1] not in SUITS:
        raise ValueError(f"bad card {text!r}: use forms like AS, 7H, 10D")
    rank = 1 if t[:-1] in ("A", "1") else int(t[:-1])
    if not 1 <= rank <= 10:
        raise ValueError(f"bad rank in {text!r}")
    return (rank, t[-1])


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- scoring

def stack_value(stack, trump_suit: str, rules: Rules = OFFICIAL) -> int:
    """Final value of a stack: trump multiplier, then x2 for each card in a pair.

    Each card is in at most one pair; with three of a rank the owner pairs the
    two highest-valued cards (the trump one, if any).
    """
    by_rank = defaultdict(list)
    for r, s in stack:
        v = r
        if s == trump_suit:
            v = v * 2 if rules.trump == "double" else v // 2
        by_rank[r].append(v)
    total = 0
    for vals in by_rank.values():
        vals.sort(reverse=True)
        paired = len(vals) // 2 * 2
        total += 2 * sum(vals[:paired]) + sum(vals[paired:])
    return total


def _exchanges(mine, theirs):
    """All single exchanges: yields ((give, get), new_mine, new_theirs)."""
    for i, give in enumerate(mine):
        for j, get in enumerate(theirs):
            m, t = list(mine), list(theirs)
            m[i], t[j] = get, give
            yield (give, get), tuple(m), tuple(t)


@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def swap_phase(s1, s2, trump_suit: str, rules: Rules = OFFICIAL):
    """Perfect swap play. Player 2 (last chooser) acts first, then Player 1.

    Returns (stack margin P1 - P2, P2 action, P1 action); an action is None
    for a pass or (card given, card received) from that player's view.
    """
    def margin(a, b):
        return stack_value(a, trump_suit, rules) - stack_value(b, trump_suit, rules)

    def p1_reply(a, b, p2_action):
        options = [(margin(a, b), None)]
        if rules.swap == "any" or p2_action is None:
            options += [(margin(na, nb), act) for act, na, nb in _exchanges(a, b)]
        else:  # "undo": Player 1 may only reverse Player 2's exchange
            give2, get2 = p2_action
            undo_a = tuple(get2 if c == give2 else c for c in a)
            undo_b = tuple(give2 if c == get2 else c for c in b)
            options.append((margin(undo_a, undo_b), (give2, get2)))
        return max(options, key=lambda o: o[0])

    candidates = [(None, s1, s2)]
    candidates += [(act, na, nb) for act, nb, na in _exchanges(s2, s1)]
    best = None
    for p2_action, a, b in candidates:
        value, p1_action = p1_reply(a, b, p2_action)
        if best is None or value < best[0]:
            best = (value, p2_action, p1_action)
    return best


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- play phase

def _choices(row, s1, s2, offerer, i):
    """The chooser's two options for the offer (row[i], row[i+1]).

    Yields (taken card, chip change P1 - P2, new row, new s1, new s2).
    """
    for k in (0, 1):
        take, stay = row[i + k], row[i + 1 - k]
        new_row = row[: i + k] + row[i + k + 1:]
        if offerer == 1:
            yield take, stay[0] - take[0], new_row, s1, tuple(sorted(s2 + (take,)))
        else:
            yield take, take[0] - stay[0], new_row, tuple(sorted(s1 + (take,))), s2


@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def value(row, s1=(), s2=(), offerer=1, rules: Rules = OFFICIAL) -> int:
    """Margin still to come (P1 - P2) from this position under perfect play."""
    if len(row) == 1:
        last = row[0]
        bonus = last[0] if offerer == 2 else -last[0]  # last offerer = the one who just moved
        return bonus + swap_phase(s1, s2, last[1], rules)[0]
    return (max if offerer == 1 else min)(
        offer_value(row, s1, s2, offerer, i, rules) for i in range(len(row) - 1)
    )


def offer_value(row, s1, s2, offerer, i, rules: Rules = OFFICIAL) -> int:
    """Value of offering (row[i], row[i+1]); the chooser replies perfectly."""
    vals = [d + value(r, a, b, 3 - offerer, rules) for _, d, r, a, b in _choices(row, s1, s2, offerer, i)]
    return min(vals) if offerer == 1 else max(vals)


def _check_even(row):
    if len(row) % 2:
        raise ValueError(
            f"solver.py handles an even number of cards only (got {len(row)}): it assumes Player 1 "
            "makes the last offer and Player 2 swaps first. For any card count, use "
            "experiments/size_shift.py, whose solver lets the last chooser swap first.")


def solve(row, rules: Rules = OFFICIAL) -> int:
    """Final margin (P1 - P2) of a deal under perfect play (even number of cards)."""
    _check_even(row)
    return value(tuple(row), (), (), 1, rules)


def opening_values(row, rules: Rules = OFFICIAL):
    """Final margin after each of Player 1's five possible opening offers."""
    _check_even(row)
    row = tuple(row)
    return [offer_value(row, (), (), 1, i, rules) for i in range(len(row) - 1)]


def principal_line(row, rules: Rules = OFFICIAL):
    """One perfect line of play as printable lines, plus the final scores."""
    _check_even(row)
    row, s1, s2, offerer = tuple(row), (), (), 1
    chips = {1: 0, 2: 0}
    out = []
    while len(row) > 1:
        pick = max if offerer == 1 else min
        i = pick(range(len(row) - 1), key=lambda j: offer_value(row, s1, s2, offerer, j, rules))
        opts = list(_choices(row, s1, s2, offerer, i))
        chooser_pick = min if offerer == 1 else max
        take, _, nrow, ns1, ns2 = chooser_pick(opts, key=lambda o: o[1] + value(o[2], o[3], o[4], 3 - offerer, rules))
        stay = row[i] if take == row[i + 1] else row[i + 1]
        chooser = 3 - offerer
        chips[chooser] += take[0]
        chips[offerer] += stay[0]
        out.append(f"P{offerer} offers {card_str(row[i])} {card_str(row[i + 1])}; "
                   f"P{chooser} takes {card_str(take)}, P{offerer} scores {card_str(stay)}   "
                   f"chips {chips[1]}-{chips[2]}")
        row, s1, s2, offerer = nrow, ns1, ns2, chooser
    last = row[0]
    chips[1] += last[0]  # Player 1 is always the last offerer with six cards
    out.append(f"Last card {card_str(last)}: trump is {SYMBOLS[last[1]]}; P1 collects {last[0]} more   "
               f"chips {chips[1]}-{chips[2]}")
    _, a2, a1 = swap_phase(s1, s2, last[1], rules)

    def show(act):
        return "pass" if act is None else f"gives {card_str(act[0])} for {card_str(act[1])}"

    out.append(f"Swap: P2 {show(a2)}; P1 {show(a1)}")
    # apply swaps to report final stacks
    if a2 is not None:
        give, get = a2
        s2 = tuple(get if c == give else c for c in s2)
        s1 = tuple(give if c == get else c for c in s1)
    if a1 is not None:
        give, get = a1
        s1 = tuple(get if c == give else c for c in s1)
        s2 = tuple(give if c == get else c for c in s2)
    t1 = chips[1] + stack_value(s1, last[1], rules)
    t2 = chips[2] + stack_value(s2, last[1], rules)
    out.append(f"Final: P1 {' '.join(map(card_str, s1))} -> {t1}   "
               f"P2 {' '.join(map(card_str, s2))} -> {t2}")
    return out, t1, t2


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- brute force check

def brute_force(row, rules: Rules = OFFICIAL) -> int:
    """Unmemoized full game-tree search, written separately, for validation."""
    def swap(s1, s2, trump):
        def m(a, b):
            return stack_value(a, trump, rules) - stack_value(b, trump, rules)

        def swaps(a, b):
            res = []
            for x in a:
                for y in b:
                    res.append((x, y,
                                [y if c == x else c for c in a],
                                [x if c == y else c for c in b]))
            return res

        p2_results = []
        p2_results.append(max([m(s1, s2)] + [m(na, nb) for _, _, na, nb in swaps(s1, s2)]))
        for x, y, nb, na in swaps(s2, s1):  # P2 gives x, gets y
            if rules.swap == "any":
                p2_results.append(max([m(na, nb)] + [m(a2, b2) for _, _, a2, b2 in swaps(na, nb)]))
            else:
                p2_results.append(max(m(na, nb), m(s1, s2)))
        return min(p2_results)

    def play(row, s1, s2, offerer, margin):
        if len(row) == 1:
            last = row[0]
            return margin + last[0] + swap(s1, s2, last[1])
        offers = []
        for i in range(len(row) - 1):
            replies = []
            for k in (0, 1):
                take, stay = row[i + k], row[i + 1 - k]
                rest = row[: i + k] + row[i + k + 1:]
                if offerer == 1:
                    replies.append(play(rest, s1, s2 + [take], 2, margin + stay[0] - take[0]))
                else:
                    replies.append(play(rest, s1 + [take], s2, 1, margin + take[0] - stay[0]))
            offers.append(min(replies) if offerer == 1 else max(replies))
        return max(offers) if offerer == 1 else min(offers)

    return play(list(row), [], [], 1, 0)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- command line

def main(argv=None):
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Exact solver for Last Suit Standing.")
    ap.add_argument("cards", nargs="*", help="six cards left to right, e.g. 3S 4D 10H 2C 7S AH")
    ap.add_argument("--deals", type=int, default=0, help="report statistics over N random deals")
    ap.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=None, help="random seed")
    ap.add_argument("--swap", choices=["any", "undo"], default="any", help="swap reading (default: any)")
    ap.add_argument("--trump", choices=["double", "half"], default="double", help="trump scoring (default: double)")
    ap.add_argument("--check", action="store_true", help="also verify the deal by brute force")
    args = ap.parse_args(argv)
    rules = Rules(swap=args.swap, trump=args.trump)
    rng = random.Random(args.seed)

    if args.deals:
        wins = ties = total = 0
        for _ in range(args.deals):
            v = solve(rng.sample(DECK, 6), rules)
            value.cache_clear()
            wins += v > 0
            ties += v == 0
            total += v
        n = args.deals
        print(f"{n} random deals, rules: swap={rules.swap}, trump={rules.trump}")
        print(f"Player 1 wins {wins / n:.1%}, ties {ties / n:.1%}, loses {(n - wins - ties) / n:.1%}; "
              f"mean margin {total / n:+.2f}")
        return 0

    if args.cards:
        if len(args.cards) != 6:
            ap.error("give exactly six cards")
        try:
            row = [parse_card(c) for c in args.cards]
        except ValueError as e:
            ap.error(str(e))
        if len(set(row)) != 6:
            ap.error("the six cards must be different")
    else:
        row = rng.sample(DECK, 6)

    print("Deal:", " ".join(map(card_str, row)), f"  (rules: swap={rules.swap}, trump={rules.trump})")
    ov = opening_values(row, rules)
    print("Value of each opening offer for P1:",
          ", ".join(f"{card_str(row[i])}{card_str(row[i + 1])} {v:+d}" for i, v in enumerate(ov)))
    lines, t1, t2 = principal_line(row, rules)
    print("Perfect play:")
    for ln in lines:
        print("  " + ln)
    v = solve(row, rules)
    result = "Player 1 wins" if v > 0 else "Player 2 wins" if v < 0 else "Tie"
    print(f"Result: {result}, margin {v:+d}")
    assert t1 - t2 == v, "internal check failed: replayed line does not match game value"
    if args.check:
        b = brute_force(row, rules)
        print(f"Brute-force check: {'passed' if b == v else 'FAILED'} ({b:+d})")
        return 0 if b == v else 1
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())
~~~~~

## File: experiments/scaling.md

~~~~~markdown
# Training-scale experiment

**Question.** Does a model that gets better at 6-card games become worse at 7-card games?

**The predictions below were written and committed before any runs.** The git history shows the commit time.

## Why ask

Earlier experiments ([size_shift.md](size_shift.md), [size_shift_followup.md](size_shift_followup.md)) suggest models learn the structure of the card count they train on, including which player has the last word, rather than the general rule. If so, more training might entrench that structure, so play at the opposite parity could get *worse* as play at the training size improves. That pattern is called inverse scaling. It matters for safety because it would mean capability on the main task and fragility in a nearby situation grow together, and a test of the main task would not reveal it.

## Design

- Models are trained on 6-card games only, with **250, 500, 1,500 or 4,000 deals**. Smaller sets are prefixes of the larger ones, using the same positions and labels.
- Two model types, each with **3 seeds** (0, 1 and 2): the MLP from `size_shift.py`, and gradient-boosted trees as in `size_shift_followup.py`.
- Testing uses 4 to 8 cards, with the same 200 held-out deals per size as the earlier experiments. The metric is points lost per game against perfect play, both seats averaged.
- **Sanity check:** the MLP at 1,500 deals with seeds 0 and 1 uses exactly the data and settings of `size_shift.py`, so it should reproduce that experiment's 6-card row (2.42 on 6, 11.05 on 7, 8.70 on 8).

## Pre-registered outcomes

All comparisons are between **250 and 4,000 deals**, per model type, using the paired difference per test deal averaged over seeds, with a bootstrap 95% CI.

- **6 cards (training size):** expected to improve. If it does not, the experiment is uninformative for that model type, because more data did not make it more capable.
- **7 cards (opposite parity), the main question.** The outcome is classified as:
  - **Inverse scaling:** the loss increases (CI entirely above 0);
  - **Flat:** the CI includes 0;
  - **Improves:** the loss decreases (CI entirely below 0).
- **8 cards (same parity):** classified the same way.

**My prediction.** For both model types: 6 cards improves; 8 cards improves; **7 cards does not improve** (flat or inverse scaling). The prediction counts as *wrong* for a model type if 7 cards improves with a CI excluding 0.

## Results

Added after the run. Raw output is in `scaling_results.txt`. The sanity check passed exactly: the MLP at 1,500 deals, seeds 0–1, gives 2.42 / 11.05 / 8.70, as in `size_shift.py`.

**Headline.** For the neural network, **more training on 6 cards made play worse at every other card count**, while 6-card play kept improving. The effect is largest and steadiest at 7 cards: the loss rose at every step, from 9.21 to 11.98 points per game, and in all three seeds. Gradient-boosted trees did **not** show this. They improved at the same parity and stayed flat at the opposite parity.

Points lost per game against perfect play, mean of seeds 0–2:

**MLP**

| 6-card training deals | 4 | 5 | *6 (trained)* | 7 | 8 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 250 | 1.41 | 3.66 | 3.18 | 9.21 | 10.13 |
| 500 | 1.46 | 3.79 | 2.65 | 10.18 | 9.74 |
| 1,500 | 1.40 | 4.28 | 2.42 | 10.97 | 9.48 |
| 4,000 | 1.72 | 4.33 | **2.03** | **11.98** | 11.38 |
| Greedy | 1.29 | 2.90 | 4.41 | 7.26 | 9.88 |

**Gradient-boosted trees**

| 6-card training deals | 4 | 5 | *6 (trained)* | 7 | 8 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 250 | 1.26 | 3.41 | 2.77 | 8.64 | 8.94 |
| 500 | 1.17 | 3.67 | 2.32 | 8.91 | 8.30 |
| 1,500 | 1.07 | 3.37 | 1.92 | 8.69 | 7.68 |
| 4,000 | 1.07 | 3.36 | **1.78** | 8.95 | 7.75 |
| Greedy | 1.29 | 2.90 | 4.41 | 7.26 | 9.88 |

**Change from 250 to 4,000 deals** (95% CI; negative means it improves), with the pre-registered classification:

| Test size | MLP | Per seed | Trees | Per seed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4 | +0.32 [+0.12, +0.51] **inverse scaling** | +0.38, +0.45, +0.13 | −0.19 [−0.30, −0.09] improves | −0.19, −0.22, −0.17 |
| 5 | +0.67 [+0.22, +1.13] **inverse scaling** | +0.88, +0.45, +0.68 | −0.05 [−0.29, +0.20] flat | −0.38, +0.01, +0.23 |
| *6 (trained)* | −1.15 [−1.48, −0.83] improves | −0.73, −1.17, −1.54 | −1.00 [−1.28, −0.71] improves | −0.95, −1.06, −0.97 |
| **7** | **+2.77 [+2.08, +3.54] inverse scaling** | +2.97, +2.25, +3.10 | +0.32 [−0.24, +0.91] flat | +0.03, +0.46, +0.46 |
| 8 | +1.25 [+0.64, +1.87] **inverse scaling** | +1.76, +2.17, −0.20 | −1.19 [−1.81, −0.57] improves | −1.18, −1.38, −1.00 |

### Scoring the predictions

| Prediction | MLP | Trees |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 6 cards improves | confirmed | confirmed |
| 8 cards improves | **wrong**: inverse scaling (2 of 3 seeds) | confirmed |
| 7 cards does not improve | confirmed: **inverse scaling** | confirmed: flat |

For trees, every prediction held. For the MLP, the main prediction held in its stronger form, and the 8-card prediction was wrong: the MLP got worse at 8 cards too.

## What this shows

1. **For the neural network, capability and fragility grew together.** Each increase in training made it better at the game it was trained on and worse at every other card count. A standard check, held-out 6-card deals, would have endorsed the 4,000-deal model as the best one. It is in fact the worst on 4, 5, 7 and 8 cards. At 7 cards it loses 65% more points than an untrained greedy player.
2. **The parity effect remains.** The damage is largest at 7 cards, the nearest size with the opposite parity, and smallest at 4.
3. **The kind of model matters.** Gradient-boosted trees trained on the same data did not degrade. They kept improving at the same parity and stayed flat at the opposite one. Whether more data entrenches a narrow solution depends on the learner, not only on the data.

The broader idea that more training can make models more specialized is familiar in machine learning. What this adds is an exact, pre-registered measurement of it, a clean case where held-out validation on the training task points the wrong way, and a contrast between two model types trained on identical data.

## Limits

Three seeds, 200 test deals per size, two model types with fixed settings, and evaluation against a perfect opponent only. The MLP's 8-card result is the least robust: one seed went the other way. The MLP uses early stopping on a 6-card validation split, so "more training" here means more data at the training size, not more epochs. Inputs use fixed card slots: at 7 and 8 cards a 6-card model reads slots it never saw filled, so part of the damage at those sizes could be an encoding artifact. At 4 and 5 cards no unseen slots are used, and the MLP still got worse. [slot_free.md](slot_free.md) tests the slots. [checkpoint.md](checkpoint.md) tests whether early stopping, rather than the amount of data, causes the 7-card damage.

## Reproduce

```bash
pip install numpy scikit-learn
python3 experiments/scaling.py --sizes 250,500,1500,4000 --seeds 0,1,2 --test-deals 200
```

This takes about 45 minutes on 2 CPU cores. For a quick check, `--sizes 20,40 --seeds 0 --test-deals 10` runs in about 15 seconds.
~~~~~

## File: experiments/scaling.py

~~~~~python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Training-scale experiment (pre-registered in scaling.md).

Does more 6-card training make play at other card counts better or worse?
Models: MLP and gradient-boosted trees, 3 seeds each, trained on the first
250 / 500 / 1,500 / 4,000 six-card deals of one fixed stream (prefixes, so
smaller sets are subsets of larger ones). Tested on 4-8 cards against
perfect play, with the same test deals as size_shift.py.

Usage: python3 experiments/scaling.py [--sizes 250,500,1500,4000] [--seeds 0,1,2] [--test-deals 200]
"""
import argparse
import os
import random
import sys
import time
import warnings

import numpy as np

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(__file__))
import size_shift as Z  # noqa: E402
from size_shift import S, SIZES  # noqa: E402
from size_shift_followup import make_model, Policy, feats_plain, test_sets, ci  # noqa: E402

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")


def stream_dataset(n_max, seed, tkeys):
    """Positions from the first n_max six-card deals, plus each deal's end index.
    Uses the same deal stream and rollout stream as size_shift.py, so the first
    1,500 deals reproduce that experiment's training data exactly."""
    rng_d = random.Random(100 * seed + 6)
    deals = [d for d in (rng_d.sample(S.DECK, 6) for _ in range(n_max)) if tuple(map(tuple, d)) not in tkeys]
    rng = random.Random(seed * 7 + 6)
    X, y, ends = [], [], []
    for d in deals:
        seen = set()
        for eps in (0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 1.0):
            for st in Z.rollout(d, eps, rng):
                if st in seen:
                    continue
                seen.add(st)
                v = Z.value(*st)
                for p in [(0, 1, 2, 3)] + [tuple(rng.sample(range(4), 4)) for _ in range(2)]:
                    X.append(feats_plain(*st, perm=p))
                    y.append(v)
        Z.clear()
        ends.append(len(y))
    return np.array(X, dtype=np.float32), np.array(y, dtype=np.float32), ends


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--sizes", default="250,500,1500,4000")
    ap.add_argument("--seeds", default="0,1,2")
    ap.add_argument("--test-deals", type=int, default=200)
    args = ap.parse_args()
    ns = [int(x) for x in args.sizes.split(",")]
    seeds = [int(x) for x in args.seeds.split(",")]
    t0 = time.time()

    tests = test_sets(args.test_deals)
    tkeys = {tuple(map(tuple, d)) for ds in tests.values() for d in ds}
    greedy = {te: Z.evaluate(Z.Greedy(), tests[te])[:, :2].mean(axis=1) for te in SIZES}

    res = {}  # (kind, n, test size) -> list over seeds of per-deal points lost
    for seed in seeds:
        X, y, ends = stream_dataset(max(ns), seed, tkeys)
        print(f"seed {seed}: {len(ends)} deals, {len(y)} positions [{time.time() - t0:.0f}s]", flush=True)
        for n in ns:
            k = ends[min(n, len(ends)) - 1]
            for kind in ("mlp", "trees"):
                pol = Policy(make_model(kind, seed).fit(X[:k], y[:k]), feats_plain)
                for te in SIZES:
                    res.setdefault((kind, n, te), []).append(Z.evaluate(pol, tests[te])[:, :2].mean(axis=1))
                print(f"  seed {seed} {kind} n={n} ({k} positions) [{time.time() - t0:.0f}s]", flush=True)

    mean = {key: np.mean(v, axis=0) for key, v in res.items()}  # per-deal, averaged over seeds
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

    for kind in ("mlp", "trees"):
        print(f"\n{kind}: points lost per game vs perfect play (mean of seeds {seeds})")
        print(f"{'deals':<10}" + "".join(f"{te:>9} cards" for te in SIZES))
        for n in ns:
            print(f"{n:<10}" + "".join(f"{mean[(kind, n, te)].mean():>15.2f}" for te in SIZES))
        print(f"{'greedy':<10}" + "".join(f"{greedy[te].mean():>15.2f}" for te in SIZES))
        lo_n, hi_n = min(ns), max(ns)
        print(f"  change from {lo_n} to {hi_n} deals (negative = improves), 95% CI:")
        for te in SIZES:
            d = mean[(kind, hi_n, te)] - mean[(kind, lo_n, te)]
            a, b = ci(d, rng)
            cls = "IMPROVES" if b < 0 else "INVERSE SCALING" if a > 0 else "flat"
            per_seed = [np.mean(res[(kind, hi_n, te)][i] - res[(kind, lo_n, te)][i]) for i in range(len(seeds))]
            print(f"    {te} cards: {d.mean():+.2f} [{a:+.2f}, {b:+.2f}] {cls}; per seed "
                  + " ".join(f"{x:+.2f}" for x in per_seed))
    if 1500 in ns and {0, 1} <= set(seeds):
        chk = {te: np.mean([res[("mlp", 1500, te)][seeds.index(s)] for s in (0, 1)], axis=0).mean() for te in (6, 7, 8)}
        print(f"\nsanity check, MLP 1500 deals seeds 0-1 (expect 2.42 / 11.05 / 8.70): "
              f"{chk[6]:.2f} / {chk[7]:.2f} / {chk[8]:.2f}")
    print(f"\ntotal time {time.time() - t0:.0f}s")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
~~~~~

## File: experiments/checkpoint.md

~~~~~markdown
# Checkpoint control

**Question.** Finding 1 says more 6-card training makes a neural net worse at other card counts. The net in that experiment stops when a 6-card validation split stops improving. This run asks whether that stopping rule is the cause. The same nets are trained for a fixed number of passes, with no early stopping, and compared at the same pass.

**The predictions below were written and committed before any runs.** The git history shows the commit time.

## Design

Same solver, deals, rollouts, suit relabelling, inputs, one-step policy, and metric as `scaling.py`. The metric is points lost per game against perfect play, both seats. Test deals are the same 200 held-out deals per size. This run tests 6, 7, and 8 cards only.

- **Data.** Nested prefixes of the scaling stream: 250, 1,000, and 4,000 six-card deals. Seeds 0, 1, 2, and 3.
- **Neural net.** The same MLP (two hidden layers, 256 and 128; Adam; learning rate 0.001; batch size 256). Early stopping is off, and the training-loss stopper is off, so every net runs for exactly 200 passes over its training rows. It trains on all of those rows. The scaling run held out 10% of the rows for stopping; this one does not.
- **Stages.** The net is tested after 10, 20, 40, 80, 160, and 200 passes. A matched stage means the same pass count.
- **Selection check.** A fixed set of 60 validation deals at each of 6, 7, and 8 cards is held out of training and out of the test set. At each stage the net's value error (mean squared error) is measured on those deals. For each seed and training size, two chosen stages are recorded: the lowest error on 6-card validation deals, and the lowest average of the three sizes' errors. Ties take the earliest stage.
- **Trees.** The same gradient-boosted trees, 500 iterations, early stopping off, on the same three prefixes and four seeds. They are tested only at the end. This is a check that they still differ from the net, not a second copy of the stage rule.
- **Intervals.** The deal comparison is the paired difference per test deal, averaged over seeds, with a bootstrap 95% CI over deals. The four seed values are reported separately and are not folded into that interval. "Rises" means the CI is entirely above 0 and at least 3 of the 4 seeds are positive. "Improves" means the CI is entirely below 0.

## Pre-registered predictions

| | Prediction | Call |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a | At pass 200, 6-card loss falls from 250 to 4,000 deals | Yes |
| b | At pass 200, 7-card loss rises from 250 to 4,000 deals | Yes |
| c | 7-card loss rises from 250 to 4,000 deals at every stage | No |
| d | The mixed-size validation choice still has higher 7-card loss at 4,000 than at 250 | No |
| e | Trees at 500 iterations: 7-card loss does not rise from 250 to 4,000 | Yes |
| f | The 6-card validation choice still has higher 7-card loss at 4,000 than at 250 | Yes |

The reason for (c) and (d): early passes have not fit the 6-card games yet, so more data should not hurt there. A check that can see 7-card value error can pick one of those earlier nets. The reason for (b) and (f): by the end, and whenever the chosen net is the one that fits 6 cards best, more 6-card data still entrenches the 6-card rule. Trees did not show that pattern when they were allowed to stop early, and (e) says they still do not.

## How finding 1 is judged

- If (a) is not observed, the neural-net run is uninformative, and finding 1 is left as it stands.
- Finding 1 stands unchanged only if 7-card loss rises at every stage.
- If it rises at pass 200 but not at every stage, the README claim is revised to the stages where it rises: more data hurts 7-card play only after the net has had those passes, not from the start of training.
- If it rises at no stage, the data-amount claim is withdrawn. The scaling result is then attributed to the stopping rule.
- If (b) is observed and (d) is not, add that a validation check which includes other card counts would not have picked the fragile net. If (f) is observed, add that a 6-card check still would have.
- If (e) is not observed, the trees no longer differ: they also get worse at 7 cards when early stopping is off.

The 1,000-deal row and the 8-card column are reported. They do not decide the finding.

## Results

Added after the run. Raw output is in `checkpoint_results.txt`. The run took 2,562 seconds. Seeds 0–2 have the same six-card position counts as `scaling_results.txt` (252,726; 253,005; 252,987).

**Six and seven cards, 4,000 deals minus 250.** Negative means play improved. "Rises" means the deal interval is entirely above 0 and at least 3 of the 4 seeds are positive.

| Pass | 6 cards | Per seed | 7 cards | Per seed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 10 | −0.92 [−1.16, −0.68] improves | −0.87, −0.89, −0.95, −0.96 | **+2.66 [+1.94, +3.42] rises** | +4.05, +2.35, +3.12, +1.14 |
| 20 | −0.99 [−1.28, −0.71] improves | −0.52, −1.08, −1.24, −1.12 | **+1.96 [+1.32, +2.64] rises** | +3.18, +2.01, +1.88, +0.76 |
| 40 | −1.13 [−1.42, −0.84] improves | −0.77, −1.18, −1.60, −0.97 | **+0.95 [+0.37, +1.53] rises** | +1.71, +1.27, +1.44, −0.64 |
| 80 | −1.38 [−1.70, −1.08] improves | −1.14, −1.29, −1.88, −1.22 | **+1.04 [+0.44, +1.64] rises** | +1.74, +2.42, −0.43, +0.42 |
| 160 | −1.59 [−1.92, −1.26] improves | −1.34, −1.64, −1.60, −1.76 | **+1.01 [+0.36, +1.67] rises** | +2.13, +1.29, +0.10, +0.53 |
| 200 | −1.79 [−2.16, −1.46] improves | −1.64, −2.11, −1.86, −1.54 | **+0.85 [+0.21, +1.51] rises** | +1.80, +0.49, +0.69, +0.42 |

At passes 40 and 80, one seed went the other way on 7 cards. The interval is still above 0, and three seeds are positive, so those stages count as a rise. The 1,000-deal loss sits between the 250 and 4,000 losses at every pass except pass 80, where 1,000 (11.85) is slightly worse than 4,000 (11.54).

**Chosen passes.** The pass with the lowest validation error, 6-card error first and mixed-size error second:

| Seed | 250 deals | 1,000 | 4,000 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 80 / 10 | 20 / 10 | 80 / 10 |
| 1 | 40 / 10 | 10 / 10 | 40 / 10 |
| 2 | 20 / 10 | 20 / 10 | 40 / 20 |
| 3 | 20 / 10 | 20 / 10 | 10 / 10 |

On 7 cards, 4,000 minus 250: the 6-card choice is +1.49 [+0.88, +2.07], seeds +1.74, +1.27, +2.71, +0.22. The mixed-size choice is +2.64 [+1.93, +3.38], seeds +4.05, +2.35, +3.04, +1.14. Mixed-size error picks an early pass, and the early pass is where the 7-card gap is largest.

**Trees**, 500 iterations, no early stopping. From 250 to 4,000 deals: 6 cards −1.01 [−1.26, −0.76]; 7 cards +0.51 [+0.02, +1.03], seeds +1.00, +0.31, +0.36, +0.39; 8 cards −1.24 [−1.73, −0.74].

Eight cards for the net is not part of the decision. It rises at pass 10 (+0.95), is flat at 20, 40, and 80, and improves at 160 and 200 (−0.81, then −1.01).

### Scored predictions

| | Observed | Call |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a | Yes | Yes |
| b | Yes | Yes |
| c | Yes | No |
| d | Yes | No |
| e | No | Yes |
| f | Yes | Yes |

(a), (b), and (f) hit. (c) missed: the 7-card loss rises at every pass, including pass 10. (d) missed: the mixed-size choice still rises, and by more than the final pass. (e) missed: the trees rise too.

### What this means under the decision rules

(a) was observed, so the run is informative. Seven-card loss rises at every matched pass, so **finding 1 stands unchanged.** The stopping rule is not the cause. At pass 10 the net trained on 4,000 deals is already better at 6 cards and worse at 7, by 2.66 points.

The mixed-size check does not remove the damage, so there is nothing to add about a broader validation check avoiding the fragile net. The 6-card check still selects a net that is worse at 7 cards.

The tree statement does not hold. With early stopping off, the trees also get worse at 7 cards, by 0.51 points, in all four seeds. That rise is smaller than the net's. In the earlier experiment, where the trees were allowed to stop early, their 7-card change was flat.

A pass is one trip through the training rows. With batch size 256, the 4,000-deal net takes about sixteen times as many Adam updates per pass as the 250-deal net (about 988 against about 62). The decision above compares matched passes. At matched update counts that rise does not survive: more deals lowered 7-card loss, and training the same 4,000-deal net longer still raised it ([matched_steps.md](matched_steps.md)).
~~~~~

## File: experiments/checkpoint.py

~~~~~python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Checkpoint control (pre-registered in checkpoint.md).

Fixed training passes, no early stopping. Predictions and decision rules
live in checkpoint.md. This file does not change them.

Quick check:
    python3 experiments/checkpoint.py --sizes 12,20 --seeds 0 --test-deals 3 --val-deals 2 --epochs 4 --stages 2,4 --tree-iters 5
Full run (writes experiments/checkpoint_results.txt):
    python3 experiments/checkpoint.py
"""
import argparse
import os
import random
import sys
import time
import warnings

import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPRegressor

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(__file__))
import size_shift as Z  # noqa: E402
from size_shift import S  # noqa: E402
from size_shift_followup import Policy, feats_plain, test_sets, ci  # noqa: E402
from scaling import stream_dataset  # noqa: E402

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

TEST_SIZES = (6, 7, 8)
# From checkpoint.md. Do not edit these to fit a run.
PREDICTIONS = (
    ("a", "At pass 200, 6-card loss falls from 250 to 4,000 deals", "Yes"),
    ("b", "At pass 200, 7-card loss rises from 250 to 4,000 deals", "Yes"),
    ("c", "7-card loss rises from 250 to 4,000 at every stage", "No"),
    ("d", "Mixed-size validation choice: 7-card loss rises from 250 to 4,000", "No"),
    ("e", "Trees, 500 iterations: 7-card loss does not rise from 250 to 4,000", "Yes"),
    ("f", "6-card validation choice: 7-card loss rises from 250 to 4,000", "Yes"),
)


class _Tee:
    def __init__(self, *streams):
        self.streams = streams

    def write(self, data):
        for s in self.streams:
            s.write(data)

    def flush(self):
        for s in self.streams:
            s.flush()


def held_out(n_each, salt):
    """Fixed deals at 6, 7, and 8 cards. Test uses salt 1000 via test_sets; validation uses 2000."""
    out = {}
    for n in TEST_SIZES:
        rng = random.Random(salt + n)
        out[n] = [rng.sample(S.DECK, n) for _ in range(n_each)]
    return out


def position_set(deals_by_size, salt):
    """Rollout positions, identity suit labels, one fixed stream per card count."""
    out = {}
    for n, deals in deals_by_size.items():
        rng = random.Random(salt + n)
        X, y = [], []
        for d in deals:
            seen = set()
            for eps in (0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 1.0):
                for st in Z.rollout(d, eps, rng):
                    if st in seen:
                        continue
                    seen.add(st)
                    X.append(feats_plain(*st))
                    y.append(Z.value(*st))
            Z.clear()
        out[n] = (np.array(X, dtype=np.float32), np.array(y, dtype=np.float32))
    return out


def make_mlp(seed):
    # n_iter_no_change and tol keep the training-loss stopper from firing before pass 200.
    return MLPRegressor(hidden_layer_sizes=(256, 128), solver="adam", learning_rate_init=1e-3,
                        batch_size=256, shuffle=True, random_state=seed, max_iter=1,
                        early_stopping=False, n_iter_no_change=10**9, tol=0.0)


def make_trees(seed, iters):
    return HistGradientBoostingRegressor(max_iter=iters, learning_rate=0.1, max_leaf_nodes=63,
                                         early_stopping=False, random_state=seed)


def mse(model, X, y):
    err = model.predict(X) - y
    return float(np.mean(err * err))


def rises(lo, per_seed):
    """CI entirely above 0, and at least 3 seeds positive. As fixed in checkpoint.md."""
    return lo > 0 and sum(x > 0 for x in per_seed) >= 3


def label(lo, hi, per_seed):
    if hi < 0:
        return "improves"
    if rises(lo, per_seed):
        return "RISES"
    if lo > 0:
        return "CI above 0"
    return "flat"


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--sizes", default="250,1000,4000")
    ap.add_argument("--seeds", default="0,1,2,3")
    ap.add_argument("--test-deals", type=int, default=200)
    ap.add_argument("--val-deals", type=int, default=60)
    ap.add_argument("--epochs", type=int, default=200)
    ap.add_argument("--stages", default="10,20,40,80,160,200")
    ap.add_argument("--tree-iters", type=int, default=500)
    args = ap.parse_args()
    ns = [int(x) for x in args.sizes.split(",")]
    seeds = [int(x) for x in args.seeds.split(",")]
    stages = [int(x) for x in args.stages.split(",")]
    if any(s > args.epochs or s < 1 for s in stages):
        raise SystemExit("every stage must be between 1 and --epochs")
    official = (ns == [250, 1000, 4000] and seeds == [0, 1, 2, 3] and args.test_deals == 200
                and args.val_deals == 60 and args.epochs == 200
                and stages == [10, 20, 40, 80, 160, 200] and args.tree_iters == 500)

    out_f = None
    if official:
        out_f = open(os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), "checkpoint_results.txt"), "w")
        sys.stdout = _Tee(sys.__stdout__, out_f)
    t0 = time.time()
    try:
        _run(ns, seeds, stages, args, official, t0)
    finally:
        sys.stdout = sys.__stdout__
        if out_f is not None:
            out_f.close()


def _run(ns, seeds, stages, args, official, t0):
    print(f"{'pre-registered run' if official else 'quick check, results not saved'}: "
          f"sizes {ns}, seeds {seeds}, stages {stages}, epochs {args.epochs}, "
          f"test {args.test_deals}, val {args.val_deals}, trees {args.tree_iters}", flush=True)
    tests = {n: test_sets(args.test_deals)[n] for n in TEST_SIZES}
    # test_sets builds 4-8; exclude every test deal, plus the validation deals, from training.
    all_tests = test_sets(args.test_deals)
    val = held_out(args.val_deals, 2000)
    tkeys = {tuple(map(tuple, d)) for ds in all_tests.values() for d in ds}
    tkeys |= {tuple(map(tuple, d)) for ds in val.values() for d in ds}
    print(f"validation positions...", flush=True)
    val_pos = position_set(val, 9000)
    for n in TEST_SIZES:
        print(f"  {n} cards: {len(val_pos[n][1])} positions", flush=True)
    greedy = {te: Z.evaluate(Z.Greedy(), tests[te])[:, :2].mean(axis=1) for te in TEST_SIZES}

    # (model, n, stage, test size) -> per seed, per deal, points lost
    res = {}
    # (selector, seed, n) -> chosen stage
    chosen = {}
    stage_set = set(stages)
    for seed in seeds:
        X, y, ends = stream_dataset(max(ns), seed, tkeys)
        print(f"seed {seed}: {len(ends)} six-card deals, {len(y)} positions [{time.time() - t0:.0f}s]", flush=True)
        for n in ns:
            k = ends[min(n, len(ends)) - 1]
            net = make_mlp(seed)
            scores6, scoresm = {}, {}
            for epoch in range(1, args.epochs + 1):
                net.partial_fit(X[:k], y[:k])
                if epoch not in stage_set:
                    continue
                for te in TEST_SIZES:
                    lost = Z.evaluate(Policy(net, feats_plain), tests[te])[:, :2].mean(axis=1)
                    res.setdefault(("mlp", n, epoch, te), []).append(lost)
                scores6[epoch] = mse(net, *val_pos[6])
                scoresm[epoch] = float(np.mean([mse(net, *val_pos[te]) for te in TEST_SIZES]))
            chosen[("six", seed, n)] = min(scores6, key=lambda s: (scores6[s], s))
            chosen[("mixed", seed, n)] = min(scoresm, key=lambda s: (scoresm[s], s))
            print(f"  seed {seed} mlp n={n} ({k} rows) chose 6-card pass {chosen[('six', seed, n)]}, "
                  f"mixed pass {chosen[('mixed', seed, n)]} [{time.time() - t0:.0f}s]", flush=True)
            trees = make_trees(seed, args.tree_iters)
            trees.fit(X[:k], y[:k])
            for te in TEST_SIZES:
                lost = Z.evaluate(Policy(trees, feats_plain), tests[te])[:, :2].mean(axis=1)
                res.setdefault(("trees", n, args.tree_iters, te), []).append(lost)
            print(f"  seed {seed} trees n={n} [{time.time() - t0:.0f}s]", flush=True)

    lo_n, hi_n = min(ns), max(ns)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

    def pack(kind, n, stage, te):
        return res[(kind, n, stage, te)]

    def contrast(rows_hi, rows_lo):
        """rows_* are lists over seeds of per-deal losses. Returns mean diff, ci, per-seed means."""
        per = [np.mean(h - lo) for h, lo in zip(rows_hi, rows_lo)]
        diff = np.mean([h - lo for h, lo in zip(rows_hi, rows_lo)], axis=0)
        a, b = ci(diff, rng)
        return diff, a, b, per

    print("\nMLP: points lost per game (mean of seeds)")
    print(f"{'pass':<8}{'deals':<10}" + "".join(f"{te:>9} cards" for te in TEST_SIZES))
    for epoch in stages:
        for n in ns:
            vals = [np.mean(pack("mlp", n, epoch, te), axis=0).mean() for te in TEST_SIZES]
            print(f"{epoch:<8}{n:<10}" + "".join(f"{v:>15.2f}" for v in vals))
        print(f"{'':<8}{'greedy':<10}" + "".join(f"{greedy[te].mean():>15.2f}" for te in TEST_SIZES))
    print(f"  change from {lo_n} to {hi_n} deals (negative = improves), 95% CI; per seed:")
    mlp_cmp = {}
    for epoch in stages:
        for te in TEST_SIZES:
            diff, a, b, per = contrast(pack("mlp", hi_n, epoch, te), pack("mlp", lo_n, epoch, te))
            mlp_cmp[(epoch, te)] = (diff, a, b, per)
            print(f"    pass {epoch} {te} cards: {diff.mean():+.2f} [{a:+.2f}, {b:+.2f}] {label(a, b, per)}; per seed "
                  + " ".join(f"{x:+.2f}" for x in per))

    print(f"\nChosen passes (6-card validation MSE, then mixed-size MSE):")
    for seed in seeds:
        bits = []
        for n in ns:
            bits.append(f"n={n}: {chosen[('six', seed, n)]}/{chosen[('mixed', seed, n)]}")
        print(f"  seed {seed} " + "  ".join(bits))

    def selected_contrast(selector, te):
        hi_rows, lo_rows = [], []
        for i, seed in enumerate(seeds):
            hi_rows.append(pack("mlp", hi_n, chosen[(selector, seed, hi_n)], te)[i])
            lo_rows.append(pack("mlp", lo_n, chosen[(selector, seed, lo_n)], te)[i])
        return contrast(hi_rows, lo_rows)

    print(f"\nSelected nets, {hi_n} minus {lo_n}, 7 cards:")
    sel = {}
    for name, key in (("6-card validation", "six"), ("mixed-size validation", "mixed")):
        diff, a, b, per = selected_contrast(key, 7)
        sel[key] = (diff, a, b, per)
        print(f"  {name}: {diff.mean():+.2f} [{a:+.2f}, {b:+.2f}] {label(a, b, per)}; per seed "
              + " ".join(f"{x:+.2f}" for x in per))

    print(f"\nTrees, {args.tree_iters} iterations, no early stopping")
    print(f"{'deals':<10}" + "".join(f"{te:>9} cards" for te in TEST_SIZES))
    for n in ns:
        vals = [np.mean(pack("trees", n, args.tree_iters, te), axis=0).mean() for te in TEST_SIZES]
        print(f"{n:<10}" + "".join(f"{v:>15.2f}" for v in vals))
    print(f"{'greedy':<10}" + "".join(f"{greedy[te].mean():>15.2f}" for te in TEST_SIZES))
    tree_cmp = {}
    print(f"  change from {lo_n} to {hi_n}:")
    for te in TEST_SIZES:
        diff, a, b, per = contrast(pack("trees", hi_n, args.tree_iters, te), pack("trees", lo_n, args.tree_iters, te))
        tree_cmp[te] = (diff, a, b, per)
        print(f"    {te} cards: {diff.mean():+.2f} [{a:+.2f}, {b:+.2f}] {label(a, b, per)}; per seed "
              + " ".join(f"{x:+.2f}" for x in per))

    print("\nPredictions (call was fixed before the run):")
    if not official:
        print("  scoring withheld: this is not the pre-registered design")
    else:
        final = stages[-1]
        observed = {
            "a": "Yes" if mlp_cmp[(final, 6)][2] < 0 else "No",
            "b": "Yes" if rises(mlp_cmp[(final, 7)][1], mlp_cmp[(final, 7)][3]) else "No",
            "c": "Yes" if all(rises(mlp_cmp[(e, 7)][1], mlp_cmp[(e, 7)][3]) for e in stages) else "No",
            "d": "Yes" if rises(sel["mixed"][1], sel["mixed"][3]) else "No",
            "e": "No" if rises(tree_cmp[7][1], tree_cmp[7][3]) else "Yes",
            "f": "Yes" if rises(sel["six"][1], sel["six"][3]) else "No",
        }
        for pid, text, call in PREDICTIONS:
            print(f"  {pid}  observed {observed[pid]:<3}  call {call:<3}  {text}")
    print(f"\ntotal time {time.time() - t0:.0f}s")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
~~~~~

## File: experiments/matched_steps.md

~~~~~markdown
# Matched Adam updates

**Question.** Finding 1, as tested in `checkpoint.md`, says that at the same training pass, more 6-card deals make 7-card play worse. A pass is one trip through the rows. With a batch size of 256, the 4,000-deal net takes about sixteen times as many Adam updates per pass as the 250-deal net. This run asks whether the 7-card rise is still there when the update counts match.

**The predictions below were written before this run.** The direction was suggested by lining up the already published pass table in `checkpoint_results.txt` at similar update counts. Those lined-up means are not a result. This run's paired intervals are the result. The git history shows the commit time.

## Design

Same solver, deals, rollouts, suit relabelling, inputs, one-step policy, and metric as `checkpoint.py`. The metric is points lost per game against perfect play, both seats. Test deals are the same 200 held-out deals per size, at 6, 7, and 8 cards. Training excludes those deals and the same 60 validation deals per size that `checkpoint.py` excluded, so the row counts should match that run. This run does not use the validation scores.

- **Data.** Nested prefixes of the scaling stream: 250, 1,000, and 4,000 six-card deals. Seeds 0, 1, 2, and 3.
- **Neural net.** The same MLP as `checkpoint.py`: two hidden layers, 256 and 128; Adam; learning rate 0.001; batch size 256. Early stopping is off, and the training-loss stopper is off. One call to `partial_fit` is one pass. An update is one Adam step on one batch, including a final short batch, so a pass contains `ceil(rows / 256)` updates.
- **Budgets.** 10,000, 20,000, and 40,000 updates. For each training set the recorded model is the first pass whose update count is at least the budget. The actual count is printed. The larger set can overshoot a budget by almost one pass. At 10,000 updates that overshoot is under about 9 percent for the 4,000-deal net, and well under that for the smaller nets.
- **Intervals.** The deal comparison is the paired difference per test deal, averaged over seeds, with a bootstrap 95% CI over deals. The four seed values are reported separately. "Improves" means the CI is entirely below 0 and at least 3 of the 4 seeds are negative. "Rises" means the CI is entirely above 0 and at least 3 of the 4 seeds are positive.

## Pre-registered predictions

| | Prediction | Call |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a | At the 10,000-update budget, 7-card loss improves from 250 deals to 4,000 | Yes |
| b | At the 20,000-update budget, 7-card loss improves from 1,000 deals to 4,000 | Yes |
| c | At the 40,000-update budget, 7-card loss improves from 1,000 deals to 4,000 | Yes |
| d | On the 4,000-deal nets, 7-card loss rises from the 10,000-update budget to the 40,000-update budget | Yes |

(a), (b), and (c) say that once the number of updates is matched, more deals help 7-card play. (d) says that training the same 4,000-deal net for longer still hurts 7-card play.

## How finding 1 is judged

- (a) decides. The 6-card and 8-card columns are reported and do not decide.
- If (a) improves, and neither (b) nor (c) rises, the claim that more deals cause the 7-card damage is withdrawn. The README then says the matched-pass rise did not survive matched updates: at the same update count, more 6-card deals lowered 7-card loss. If (d) also rises, add that training the 4,000-deal net longer still made 7-card play worse.
- If (a) improves but (b) or (c) rises, the direction depends on the budget. No single rewrite. The data-amount sentence stays undecided.
- If (a) rises, the data-amount claim stands at matched updates, and the README says so.
- If (a) is neither a rise nor an improvement, this test does not decide. The README keeps the note that the checkpoint comparison did not separate deals from updates.

## Results

Added after the run. Raw output is in `matched_steps_results.txt`. The run took 489 seconds. The six-card position counts match `checkpoint_results.txt` (252,726; 253,005; 252,987; 252,357).

Update counts are the first pass at or above the budget. At the 10,000 budget the 4,000-deal nets were recorded at about 10,868 updates, and the 250-deal nets at about 10,037.

**Seven cards, mean of seeds 0–3.** Negative means the larger training set, or the later budget, lost fewer points.

| Comparison | Change | Per seed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a 4,000 minus 250, about 10,000 updates | **−0.99 [−1.69, −0.27] improves** | +1.15, −1.94, −1.49, −1.69 |
| b 4,000 minus 1,000, about 20,000 updates | **−0.93 [−1.63, −0.25] improves** | −0.27, −0.10, −1.93, −1.44 |
| c 4,000 minus 1,000, about 40,000 updates | **−0.93 [−1.54, −0.31] improves** | +0.92, −0.78, −1.52, −2.35 |
| d 4,000 deals, 40,000 minus 10,000 updates | **+0.61 [+0.17, +1.06] rises** | +0.24, +1.43, +0.38, +0.40 |

On (a) and (c), seed 0 went the other way. Three seeds are negative, and the interval is below 0, so both still count as an improvement.

Absolute 7-card losses at about 10,000 updates were 11.45, 10.51, and 10.46 for 250, 1,000, and 4,000 deals. At about 40,000 updates they were 12.70, 12.01, and 11.07.

Six and eight cards do not decide. At about 10,000 updates, 4,000 minus 250 was −1.68 [−1.99, −1.40] on 6 cards and −3.85 [−4.47, −3.23] on 8 cards.

### Scored predictions

| | Observed | Call |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a | Yes | Yes |
| b | Yes | Yes |
| c | Yes | Yes |
| d | Yes | Yes |

All four hit.

### What this means under the decision rules

(a) improves, and neither (b) nor (c) rises. The claim that more deals cause the 7-card damage is withdrawn. At a matched update count, more 6-card deals lowered 7-card loss. (d) rises, so the README also says that training the 4,000-deal net longer still made 7-card play worse. The matched-pass rise in `checkpoint.md` stands as a result about passes. It is not a result about the number of deals.
~~~~~
